newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai ban on baht remittance seen hurting bourse.
newsitem.headline: Thai ban on baht remittance seen hurting bourse.

text.p: Thailand's moves to stop foreign stock investors from repatriating the Thai baht could dampen sentiment on the already plunging bourse, brokers and analysts said.

They told Reuters the Bank of Thailand's decision to plug loopholes by which speculators raise baht funds through the stock exchange may stop short-term foreign liquidation of Thai stocks but at the same time it damaged Thailand's image as a finance centre.
The stock market, already at eight-year lows, could take a further hit, they added.

"The measures will have obvious ramifications. They will in the long run become a big stumbling block for foreign investment... People do not welcome these fast and loose regulations," said a foreign analyst who requested anonymity.

The central bank on Tuesday instructed bank custodians not to accept transfers of borrowed and unpaid-for stocks among non-resident investors and it said those selling stocks could only repatriate funds in foreign currencies.
The bank's move was designed to deny speculators access to baht funds, much in demand for squaring baht/dollar positions taken in mid-May when the currency was under attack.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan reiterated on Wednesday that the measures were only temporary.

"But they leave people wondering what will happen next," a foreign analyst said. "In addition to economic and corporate risks, we now have this currency uncertainty which will further make it not worth the risk to invest here."
A central bank official told Reuters the measures sought to stop only what she called clean transfers of baht funds unrelated to normal business or investment transactions.
She said foreign investors could freely keep baht funds obtained from securities sales in Thai bank accounts or reinvest them in other business in Thailand.
Brokers said foreign stock transactions had been affected since last Thursday. The measures frustrated those hoping to remit baht funds after actively selling Thai securities on Friday and Monday.
Thailand's two-tier baht exchange rate system, adopted last month to block supply of the currency for speculators, has helped the baht rally sharply in offshore markets.

Investors seek to remit baht abroad to make gains from offshore trading at higher levels than in the domestic market. The offshore level was about 23.900 to the dollar on Wednesday against 25.720 in the domestic market.
"We don't mind if the government deals with foreign speculators betting against the baht but why should the stock market be made to suffer?" a Thai broker said.

A Thai broker estimated that foreigners who liquidated stocks in the last few days in order to arbitrage on the wide spread of onshore/offshore baht stood to lose about $20 million of potential foreign exchange gains that they would have made without the government measures.
"Somebody will have to take the hit, either the custodians or brokers. Normally the custodians fix the exchange rate for this sort of deal," the foreign analyst said.

He said the measures would likely hurt Japanese investment in Thai stocks as the ban on baht remittances clashed with Japanese regulations which require currency conversion of funds obtained from equity investment be made in Japan.
Most brokers said they expected Thailand to wait for the current spread of offshore/onshore baht to narrow before lifting the ban on baht repatriation.
But they said the Thai move to block foreign short sales of Thai stocks, by banning transfers of unpaid securities, would likely be made more permanent.
